lines.text: In 1963, a man in central Turkey knocked down a wall in his basement.
Behind it, there was a draft of cold air... and a dark passage going down.
He followed it. And it kept going. Down. And down. And down.
What he had found was not a cellar. It was a city.
At least eight levels deep, with room for twenty thousand people... and their animals.
And it had been hidden right under everyone's feet for centuries.
Not a castle. Not a fortress. A city... built downward.
This is Derinkuyu. And the real question is not how they built it... but what they were so afraid of.
Derinkuyu is a small town in Cappadocia, in the heart of Anatolia.
A land of strange rock towers, cave houses and valleys that look like another planet.
Millions of years ago, volcanoes like Erciyes and Hasan buried this whole region in ash.
The ground here is volcanic tuff: ash from ancient eruptions, pressed into soft stone.
You can carve it with simple iron tools. And when air touches it, it slowly hardens.
So for thousands of years, people here didn't build with stone. They carved into it.
Houses, churches, pigeon houses... all cut out of the cliffs.
But Derinkuyu went further. It went down.
The local story says the man's chickens kept disappearing into a crack in the wall.
Whatever the reason, when he broke through, he found tunnel after tunnel.
Archaeologists came. They cleared rubble that had sealed the passages for decades.
Six years later, in 1969, the city opened to visitors.
And even today, only part of it can be visited.
In ancient times, the town had a Greek name: Malakopea.
Let's go down, level by level.
The entrance looks like nothing. A small doorway in the ground.
Then the temperature drops. Down here it stays cool all year, around thirteen to fifteen degrees.
Near the surface: stables. Animals lived closest to the light.
Animals gave warmth, milk and food... and they were too valuable to leave outside during an attack.
Then rooms for living and sleeping, carved straight out of the rock.
Many of the old houses in the town are said to have had their own hidden way down.
In an attack, a family could disappear in minutes... and the house above would look empty.
Look at the walls: small niches, carved to hold oil lamps.
This was the only light. Tiny flames, deep under the earth.
Kitchens, with ceilings still black from smoke.
Smoke had to go somewhere, so the cooks worked close to the air shafts.
Wine and oil presses. Storage rooms for grain.
Grapes from the valleys above became wine down here, far from the summer heat.
Wells, so the city never had to come up for water.
Wider halls where people could gather, study, or pray.
On the second level, there is a long hall with a vaulted ceiling. Guides call it the school.
And near the bottom, a cross-shaped room, which many believe was a church.
The deepest point reaches around eighty-five meters.
Deeper than a twenty-story building... all dug by hand.
Getting between levels means narrow, steep stairs. Often you have to bend almost in half.
That was not bad design. It was the point.
Because Derinkuyu was not built for comfort. It was built to survive an attack.
Look at these: huge round stones, like millstones, standing next to the doorways.
Each one weighs hundreds of kilograms.
When danger came, people rolled them across the passage... from the inside.
Each level could be sealed on its own.
Imagine an enemy soldier, holding a torch, crawling into this passage.
He reaches the stone. Behind it, he hears nothing.
From outside, there was no way to move them. No handle. Nothing to grab.
The corridors are narrow, so attackers had to come one at a time, bent over, in the dark.
Some passages even have small holes in the ceiling, maybe for watching... or for attacking from above.
And breathing was solved too: dozens of ventilation shafts run from the surface to the deepest floors.
More than fifty of them have been found.
Some of these shafts also reached groundwater, working as wells.
Fresh air, water, food, animals... a whole town could disappear underground for weeks.
Think about what that means. No sunlight. Only lamps, whispers... and waiting.
Some say the city could hold out for months.
So who started digging? Nobody knows for sure.
Some researchers point to the Phrygians, around the eighth to seventh century BC.
Around 400 BC, the Greek writer Xenophon described people in Anatolia living in underground houses with their animals.
He wrote that their houses were dug into the ground, with entrances like wells, and animals living below with the people.
He didn't name Derinkuyu. But it shows the idea is very, very old.
Later, in the Byzantine era, these cities grew bigger.
For centuries, Cappadocia was a borderland between the Byzantine Empire and Arab armies.
Raids came again and again. And every time, people went underground.
Christians of the region hid here during raids and wars, for hundreds of years.
Each generation dug a little deeper, a little wider.
And think about the digging itself.
Every room, every stair, every shaft was cut by hand.
All that stone had to be carried up to the surface, basket by basket.
Where did it go? Some think it was spread over the fields, or used for the houses above. No one knows for sure.
It probably took many generations, maybe hundreds of years, to reach this depth.
And Derinkuyu is not alone. Cappadocia has many underground cities.
Researchers have counted more than two hundred underground settlements across the region.
One of them, Kaymakli, is less than ten kilometers away. Some believe a tunnel once connected the two.
If that's true... this was not a single shelter. It was an underground network.
And the story doesn't end there.
In 2014, workers on a construction project in the city of Nevşehir broke into another huge underground city.
Early reports said it might be even bigger than Derinkuyu. It is still being studied.
People used these tunnels until the twentieth century.
In 1923, after the population exchange between Turkey and Greece, the Greek Orthodox families of Derinkuyu left.
They took their memories with them... and the town above slowly forgot what was below.
Muslim families arriving from Greece settled in towns across the region, in houses they had never seen before.
Many of them had no idea what was under their feet.
The town above changed. The tunnels below fell silent.
Passages filled with dust and rubble... and the city was forgotten.
Until that one wall came down in 1963.
Since 1985, the area has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site: Göreme National Park and the rock sites of Cappadocia.
Today, you can walk down the same stairs where families once waited in the dark.
Most visitors walk through in less than an hour.
The air is still. The walls still carry the marks of tools, swung more than a thousand years ago.
You can touch the stone doors they rolled shut, and listen.
Imagine twenty thousand people, holding their breath, while someone searches the fields above.
Derinkuyu was built by fear. But it kept people alive.
And here's what still keeps archaeologists awake: large parts of it have never been fully explored.
And under Cappadocia, there may be more cities that no one has found yet.
If you could go down one more level... would you?
Tell me in the comments. And if you want the next lost place in Turkey, you know what to do.
